nameStory: The Palm Millipede gets its curious name from its tendency to be found in association with palm trees in warmer climates, though here in New England you're more likely to spot one under a maple leaf! The scientific name 'palmatus' does indeed refer to palms, reflecting this species' original discovery in Mediterranean regions where it lived among date palms.
description: The Palm Millipede is a slender, thread-like creature that looks almost like a tiny white or pale yellow earthworm with legs. These delicate millipedes are quite small, typically reaching only about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long. Unlike their chunkier millipede cousins, Palm Millipedes have an almost translucent appearance and move with a graceful, wave-like motion through leaf litter and soil. *Note: This species has very few confirmed observations in New England, so details about local populations are limited.*

idTips.label: Thread-like body
idTips.description: Extremely slender and cylindrical, feeling almost like a soft piece of white thread when gently touched - much thinner than common garden millipedes

idTips.label: Pale coloration
idTips.description: Whitish to pale yellow color with a slightly translucent quality, sometimes appearing almost ghostly in dim light

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Only about 1/2 to 3/4 inch long when fully grown, easily fitting on your thumbnail with room to spare

idTips.label: Smooth texture
idTips.description: Body feels remarkably smooth and soft to the touch, lacking the rigid segments of larger millipede species

idTips.label: Graceful movement
idTips.description: Moves in flowing, wave-like undulations rather than the stiff, mechanical crawl of larger millipedes

habitat: Palm Millipedes in New England are typically found in moist, rich soil under decomposing leaves, particularly in well-established gardens and wooded areas with deep leaf litter. They prefer areas with consistent moisture and organic matter, often near compost piles or in the rich humus layer of mature forests. *Given the limited observation data, their exact habitat preferences in our region may differ from populations elsewhere.*

seasonality.spring: Most active as soil warms and moisture levels are high from snowmelt. Look for them when turning over damp leaf litter in April and May.
seasonality.summer: May retreat deeper into soil during dry spells, but can be found near the surface after rain showers in moist, shaded areas.
seasonality.fall: Often more visible as they move through fresh leaf fall, particularly active during the cool, damp days of October and November.
seasonality.winter: Likely dormant deep in soil below frost line, though very little is known about their cold-weather behavior in New England.

funFact: Despite being called the Palm Millipede, this tiny creature is actually helping to break down New England's maple and oak leaves just as effectively as it would palm fronds in warmer climates - it's like having a tropical decomposer working in your backyard!
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for tiny white earthworms or thread worms, but Palm Millipedes have many tiny legs along their sides (look closely with a magnifying glass) while worms have none. Remember: 'Millipede has legs to spare, worms are smooth without a hair.'
contextualKnowledge: Palm Millipedes are likely introduced species in New England, possibly arriving with imported plants or soil. Their extreme rarity here suggests they may struggle with our climate, making any sighting particularly noteworthy for local naturalists.
compareHints: Since this is the only Choneiulus species reported in New England, compare it with other thin snake millipedes in the Blaniulidae family. Palm Millipedes are generally paler and more translucent than most relatives, and their thread-like thinness makes them stand out even among other slender millipede species. Most other New England millipedes are noticeably thicker and darker in color.
